coaching.title: Food for Iron
coaching.detail: Because your Ferritin is low. Lean red meat, poultry, shellfish (heme iron) — Heme iron from animal foods is absorbed far better than plant iron; a couple of servings a week helps rebuild stores. Legumes, lentils, tofu, dark leafy greens (non-heme iron) — Pair plant iron with a vitamin-C food (citrus, peppers, tomatoes) in the same meal to boost absorption. A vitamin-C food in the same meal (and avoiding tea/coffee with it) meaningfully raises non-heme iron absorption.
coaching.evidence: Low ferritin/iron responds to dietary iron; heme iron (meat) is best absorbed, and pairing plant iron with vitamin C markedly improves uptake. Source: NIH ODS Iron fact sheet.

coaching.title: Food for Vitamin D
coaching.detail: Because your Vitamin D, 25-Hydroxy is low. Fatty fish, egg yolks, and fortified milk/cereals — Fatty fish and fortified foods add some vitamin D, but food alone rarely corrects a real deficiency. Food is a MINOR lever for vitamin D — sunlight and supplements dominate. A flagged-low 25-OH-D usually needs sun exposure or a supplement, not just diet.
coaching.evidence: Few foods contain much vitamin D; fatty fish and fortified products are the main dietary sources. Source: NIH ODS Vitamin D fact sheet.

coachingAltDisplay.title: Food for Soluble fiber
coachingAltDisplay.detail: Because your LDL Cholesterol is high. Oats and barley — whole grains rich in beta-glucan — A daily bowl of oats or barley is the beta-glucan source the health claims are written for. Legumes — beans, lentils, and chickpeas — Half a cup of cooked legumes adds soluble fiber alongside plant protein. Berries and other whole fruit — Pectin-rich fruit — berries, apples, citrus — rounds out soluble fiber. Raise fiber gradually and drink more water alongside it. This complements — never replaces — whatever your clinician prescribes for cholesterol.
coachingAltDisplay.evidence: Soluble fiber lowers LDL cholesterol modestly and reliably: soluble fiber from oats and psyllium carries an FDA-authorized health claim for reduced coronary heart disease risk, and beta-glucan carries approved EFSA cholesterol claims. Source: FDA 21 CFR 101.81 (soluble fiber from certain foods and risk of CHD); EFSA-approved beta-glucan health claims.

coachingAltDisplay.title: Cut back for LDL cholesterol / ApoB
coachingAltDisplay.detail: Because your LDL Cholesterol is high. Fried and deep-fried foods — Cutting back on fried food lowers the saturated and trans fat that raises LDL and ApoB. Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish) lowers LDL more than simply cutting total fat.

coaching.title: Food for Iron
coaching.detail: Because your Ferritin is low. Lean red meat, poultry, shellfish (heme iron) — Heme iron from animal foods is absorbed far better than plant iron; a couple of servings a week helps rebuild stores. Legumes, lentils, tofu, dark leafy greens (non-heme iron) — Pair plant iron with a vitamin-C food (citrus, peppers, tomatoes) in the same meal to boost absorption. A vitamin-C food in the same meal (and avoiding tea/coffee with it) meaningfully raises non-heme iron absorption.
coaching.evidence: Low ferritin/iron responds to dietary iron; heme iron (meat) is best absorbed, and pairing plant iron with vitamin C markedly improves uptake. Source: NIH ODS Iron fact sheet.

buildFoodSuggestionFindings.title: Food for Iron
buildFoodSuggestionFindings.detail: Because your Ferritin is low. Lean red meat, poultry, shellfish (heme iron) — Heme iron from animal foods is absorbed far better than plant iron; a couple of servings a week helps rebuild stores. Legumes, lentils, tofu, dark leafy greens (non-heme iron) — Pair plant iron with a vitamin-C food (citrus, peppers, tomatoes) in the same meal to boost absorption. A vitamin-C food in the same meal (and avoiding tea/coffee with it) meaningfully raises non-heme iron absorption.
buildFoodSuggestionFindings.evidence: Low ferritin/iron responds to dietary iron; heme iron (meat) is best absorbed, and pairing plant iron with vitamin C markedly improves uptake. Source: NIH ODS Iron fact sheet.
